text: In the autumn of 1908, white homeowners in Hyde Park formed the Hyde Park Improvement Protective Club.
A prominent attorney named Francis Harper led it.
Within a short time it counted 350 members, and the historian Allan Spear notes they included some of the wealthiest dwellers on the South Side.
They were the lawyers, the businessmen, and the property owners who ran the neighborhood, and they had decided that Hyde Park would be a white neighborhood and would stay that way.
A few hundred Black families had begun to settle near Lake Avenue.
The club set out to undo that, block by block.
The club appointed a committee to buy up property owned by Black residents on white blocks.
It offered cash bonuses to Black renters who would give up their leases and leave.
And it threatened to blacklist any real estate firm that dared to sell or rent to a Black family across the line it had drawn.
Within a couple of years the club itself faded, but it had already done its work.
The small Black community along Lake Avenue shrank, and the rest of Hyde Park stayed white for the next forty years.
